utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the learned friends of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we admit the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Usher, Madam Usher, please, could you escort the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your examination-in-chief. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, if at any time there is a problem with the interpretation, please draw our attention straightaway, like you did yesterday. Examined by Mr. Wubben: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic. Yesterday, we addressed the issue of the staff of the Srebrenica armed forces local units, local commanders. My question refers now to communications. My first question is: Did Naser Oric communicate with the commanders of local units in a certain way or manner? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the commanders occasionally came by for meetings, or to seek assistance, to organise the Defence of their own villages or whichever areas they happened to be living in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when these offensives, in fact, took place and were implemented, did Naser Oric also communicate with those commanders involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what offensives my learned friend is referring to. The witness hasn't referred to any offensives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is right. There hasn't been any particular reference to any offensives. There are in the statement, but not in the testimony so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a case of rephrasing your question, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to operations in the field, organising the defence, did Naser Oric contact or communicate in a certain way with his -- with the local commanders?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question. I did not take part in any offensives, nor do I know how communications were organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any reports between Naser Oric and his commanders when it comes to these kinds of operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, "his commanders," again, the witness hasn't said that Naser Oric had any commanders, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also the word "reports." You need to explain the two things. First of all, who are supposed to be Naser Oric's commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because so far, yesterday, we had information from the witness explaining that within the Srebrenica area, it seemed that, according to him, Naser Oric was at the top, subject only to the War Presidency. That's how I understood it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's a fair summary of the evidence either. He referred to an Osman Osmanovic whose hierarchial superior was Naser Oric, and he referred to the War Presidency which was the supreme authority. But he didn't suggest at any stage that any particular commanders, or indeed any commanders as such, were under Naser Oric. That's not evidence he's given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no he did say specifically that Osmanovic was under Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. That's the only person, Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the question is this: But you are now referring to his commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also reports -- also reports. I mean, what kind of -- what do you mean by reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Was there any type of radio communication facility in -- within the Srebrenica armed forces.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any radio communication equipment that the armed forces in Srebrenica had. I only know about one particular radio device that I occasionally used to communicate with my own family in Tuzla. This piece of equipment was also used by other citizens of Srebrenica to communicate with their families outside in Tuzla. This was in the post office building, across the way from the hospital. As for any other means of communication or radio communications, this is really not something that I can talk about. I'm just not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the next military level of command in the reporting -- in a reporting procedure beyond the Srebrenica armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. You mean the civilian sector? If you're referring to something that is outside the armed forces or beyond the Srebrenica armed forces, you probably have the civilian authorities in mind, don't you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, let me ask you the next question in that respect and we'll come to that later. Was the Srebrenica armed forces part of a wider army structure?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that either. Yesterday, I said in my testimony that the defence of Srebrenica was structured in such a way as to have local units, people who had a self-organised group. If this was a rather small village, they had a company-sized group; if it was a major village, they had a battalion-sized unit. People appointed some persons with a good reputation as leaders, as unit commanders. And in actual fact, the whole area of the free Srebrenica municipality worked in this way, in terms of how people defended themselves. There was no specific organised military formation or unit in the area. The units bore the names of their commanders. For example, the area commanded by Zulfo Tursunovic, the unit in that area, was simply referred to as Zulfo's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't see why this witness is being interrupted. This witness was giving a fairly detailed and I would say important answer about how units were organised, in answer to my learned friend's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think he has stated enough the gist or the substance of the point he wanted to make had already been made, so he didn't need to go into details like Zulfo's unit and all that. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Was the Srebrenica armed forces part of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question to answer. There was no physical communication between Sarajevo as the seat of the headquarters on the one hand, and Srebrenica on the other. It wasn't possible to communicate, and it wasn't possible to go from Sarajevo to Srebrenica, or vice versa. Therefore, I can say nothing about how the system worked. There were no supplies coming from Sarajevo in terms of materiel and equipment to defend the town of Srebrenica, or medicines for that matter. No supplies. So the question is: Were the Srebrenica armed forces part of the larger framework? It strikes me as possible, but certainly there was no communication going on to confirm that. If, for example, you look at the fact that throughout the existence of the Srebrenica enclave, that means until as late as July 1995, there was not a single official visit to Srebrenica by anyone from the military or political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps this should allow you to draw your own conclusions as to what system of subordination, what chain of command, and what hierarchy exactly was in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, when you refer to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. You told us yesterday that, pretty soon after you arrived in Srebrenica, you were appointed as chief medical commander of armed forces in Srebrenica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who appointed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Osman Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you also stated at one time during your interview with the Office of the Prosecution that, before you proceeded -- you ultimately managed -- succeeded in reaching Srebrenica, on one occasion you went to the 4th Tactical Group command. What command was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This command formed part of the district staff of the Tuzla Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it fell under whose jurisdiction? Did it form part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence forces, more specifically Tuzla district staff. It was based in Kalesija municipality, 20 kilometres east of the town of Tuzla, in the direction of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. He's back to you, Mr. Wubben. I will not ask further questions on this, because he is your witness, not ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, you referred to Sarajevo. What do you mean by "Sarajevo"? Do you mean a command staff over there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the headquarters in Sarajevo. I mean the political leadership, the supreme command or, rather, the War Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in command of the headquarters of the republic army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was at the time. I know that later on Sefer Halilovic became commander. I'm not sure about the time under consideration now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can it be that in August 1992, Sefer Halilovic was chief of supreme command staff in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I'm not sure whether, indeed, he was as early as August. I know that he was appointed sometime later on, but I'm sure that should be easy enough for you to verify. There was a quick succession of different commanders in the early days, and it's impossible for me to say exactly when Sefer Halilovic was appointed as chief of staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides this high level of supreme command in Sarajevo, was there also a regional, second level of command?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were district staffs. Tuzla, for example, was one such district staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the corps that was operating in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the month of August. That was no corps, it was just Tuzla district TO, Territorial Defence. The corps was set up later on. It was called the 2nd Corps, and it was part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wasn't part of the Territorial Defence structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the 2nd Corps a kind of second level with regard to the armed forces of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly whether it was the 2nd Corps that was superior to Srebrenica. I can only say that it was Srebrenica's superior following demilitarisation. Srebrenica then fell under the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, but we're talking about after 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Hazim Sadic. In 1994, he was succeeded by Brigadier Sead Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to Hazim Sadic, was there any commander of the district or commander of the 2nd Corps? Can you name that commander?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Knez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in -- at the times that you were in Srebrenica, August 1992 till April 1993, are you aware that Naser Oric reported towards Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Are you -- if," "are you aware that" is asserting a fact and putting -- putting it into this witness' mouth that that communication occurred. It should be whether -- whether there were any communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. You have to rephrase, you need to rephrase your question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica in your time from August 1992 until April 1993, do you know whether or not Naser Oric reported to Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether he reported to him, but I know that we were all adamant that assistance should be sent to Srebrenica. Both the 2nd Corps, the Tuzla-based 2nd Corps, and the supreme command in Sarajevo, we insisted that they should send assistance in medicines and equipment so that the enclave could be defended and people could survive. I know nothing about reports because I never saw any official reports. There were reports that were conveyed by Mr. Ibrahim Becirevic, using the radio device that I mentioned. He addressed the public through Radio Sarajevo and TV Sarajevo, later to become TV Bosnia-Herzegovina. He addressed the public to inform them about the situation in Srebrenica in terms of the living conditions, in terms of the attacks, in terms of the shelling, and to tell them about the mounting numbers of those who were killed and wounded. They could watch it every night on the news. There was an update on the situation. If that's what you mean when you say "reports," yes, there were such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what time do you know what Mr. Becirevic gave those updates through these radio communications?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard such reports even before I arrived in Srebrenica. On the menus of Radio Sarajevo, to become Radio Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on TV Sarajevo, later to become TV Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I say, this was on the news for the general public. He described the situation and the conditions of life in the territory of the Srebrenica enclave. This started maybe in April 1992 or May 1992, and all throughout the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, these reports could be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were regular reports on a daily, weekly, or a month basis? Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not every day, from time to time. However, if something important happened, for example, the offensive on Srebrenica in April 1993 -- actually, from February 1993 up to the 17th of April, 1993, every day the general public was informed about what was going on in Srebrenica. Prior to that, there were regular reports once or twice a week, depending on the events which took place in Srebrenica. Such reports were sent from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from other towns. Everybody could listen in the evening and hear what was happening in Travnik, Sarajevo, Tuzla, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next is the documents I would like to show you, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please, usher. And Your Honours, I have an English translation available. I would like to tender that as well, and I would like to ask to the usher to put one English translation on the ELMO because we don't -- we are not able to present it on Sanction. The exhibit number is P69 -- sorry, 269, translation -- and the ERN number is 01801592. It's a -- I can hardly read it, Your Honour. We have to be specific and careful with this ERN number because it's hard to read. Sorry, 01 -- I'll start over again. ERN number 01801582. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, will you please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recognise this signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see it on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Because we have been given the translation so we don't have the original.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature differs from the signatures that I saw previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, because this is interesting. In what way does it differ, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It contains both the first name and the last name -- actually, the last name and the first name, unlike the signatures that I saw before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And if you look at the first part of that signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- if the witness doesn't find this signature familiar, then he's then invited to look at strokes and all the rest of it, isn't he being treated as an expert -- handwriting expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not treating him as an expert, Mr. Jones. Please let me finish my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just don't want him to be induced to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not being induced, Mr. Jones. I take objection at the way you are reacting, Mr. Jones. That is why I precisely asked him where -- why does he think that this is different from the other -- from the other signatures he has been shown, and he explains that the difference lies in that there is the first and the second. So now I'm going to ask him about the first part of that signature. Look at the first signature and forget that there is a second part, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reminds me of Naser Oric's signature, but this is not what I saw in the past. If you look at some other signatures and compare them to this one, you'll see it yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough. That's exactly what I wanted to know from you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, do you know whether or not someone signed or used to sign on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one further question: If anyone signed for someone else in your country, it would put it "za," wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise it would be forging the signature of that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you put "za" and then you signed your own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, let me address to the text of this document. It's dated the 23rd of June 1992, so before your arrival, as I may conclude. It's addressed to the republican staff, Sarajevo, and I quote only -- I will quote only the first sentence: "After the action of 21 April 1992 carried out in Potocari, 14 members of Arkan's unit were killed," and there's something illegible in my translation, "himself was wounded and later succumbed to his wounds."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, are you familiar -- do you know this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be more specific. Are you asking me whether I am familiar with the report or whether I am familiar with the event? What is it that you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, I'm going to stop your questioning for the time being and I'm going to ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a while so that we discuss something in relation to this document. It cannot be discussed in the presence of the witness. I'll explain to you later, Mr. -- Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, correct me if I'm wrong, I may have absolutely the wrong impression, but this document we have seen already in the beginning of the trial when we had the expert, the handwriting expert, testifying here. And I am under the impression, but again this is something that can be verified, that this was one of the few documents which he considered as unreliable as far as signature is concerned. I think his report, I think we need to find out, because if this is a document that, according to the handwriting expert, contains a forged signature, then we have a problem with to what extent you should, as Prosecutor, be able to use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I check, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we need to check. But I'm not in a position here and now to remember what the expert had said. If I remember well, the handwriting expert had clearly said that this is one of the documents where definitely the signature does not tally. But it features in the report. There was a comparison made between specimen signatures that the expert was told definitely belonged to Naser Oric and signatures as they appear on various documents that the Prosecution intended to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to my information, there was no opinion from the forensic analysis, and it was document Q11, so questioned document number 11. But I will further check that out to confirm to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I doubt it. Do you have a record, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I remember it was a bit more complex than that. He recognised that the -- that it was different from the others in that it had the full name and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was one part. But there was also something about the first part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The quality was too poor to actually enable examination to be carried out, and we're just checking if there was further testimony on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If we can verify this before we proceed, I think it's very important, because I will not allow the Prosecution to make use documents that are definitely forged, except insofar as they may be relevant to prove that they are forged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I'm obliged, Your Honour. Yes, Mr. Roberts, have you discovered anything -- except I'm not asking you to give me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we please have five minutes' break and that will enable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's have a five-minute break. I think it's very important. --- Break taken at 9.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We checked -- I checked, together with my staff as well, and it seems that the handwriting expert was not prepared to say that the signature constituted a forgery, and he left it at that. So we are back to square one. Mr. Wubben, I don't think I need confirmation of what I have said. You may proceed with the questions as soon as we get the witness in. Yes, Madam Usher. Thank you for your patience and your cooperation, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just add to the record that it was Q6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Q6, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it was one signature where no opinion could be expressed. And I think for the stamp also, there was insufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was a difference consisting in the extra and also the two lines inside the O --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which were commented upon by the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, from my side I can also confirm that that leaves authentication open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, if I could invite you to cut down a little bit and try to speed up, because we are moving very, very slowly. I mean, believe me, I have enough experience to know that I think it's difficult to see you finishing the examination-in-chief by Thursday, the way we are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'll try to speed up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to concentrate on -- there's so much information that this witness mentions or gives in his statements that we have barely started, we've barely started. Yes. Dr. Mujkanovic, let me explain. We needed to discuss a little bit a procedural matter relating to the document that you were shown before, before you could be asked further questions on it. We have come to our conclusion, and Mr. Wubben may proceed with his questions. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, referring now to the first part of the report, the first sentence, as read by you, can you confirm that you were aware, when you were in Srebrenica, of information like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what information Mr. Wubben is referring to or what the questions means. This is months before the witness arrived. It's really unclear to me what -- what's being sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I read out -- I read out the sentence, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose you need to read it out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read it, Dr. Mujkanovic. "After the action of 21 April 1992 carried out in Potocari, 14 members of the Arkan unit were killed and," illegible in my translation, the English, "himself was wounded and later succumbed to his wounds." Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware of any such information at your time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At your time? What do you mean? Because he wasn't in Srebrenica, so you can't tell him at your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: At your time in Srebrenica, meaning from August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Did you come to know about this event that is reported in the first paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After my arrival, I learned about this because people said that a group of Arkan's men had been intercepted on their way from Bratunac to Srebrenica. They said that 14 of Arkan's men were killed in combat, allegedly including Arkan himself, who was, people said, first wounded and then died. And then for one year after that, people believed that Arkan was dead. But a year later, he appeared in public for the first time after this incident, and then everyone realised that he had not been killed. But this is definitely something that people talked about at the time, and everyone was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, usher, P111, ERN number 026 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document, are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It has already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Meaning the prior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the one we've just finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. E, E, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For the next document, Your Honour, the English version will be on Sanction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For the next document, Your Honour, the English version is on Sanction. The document is P111. The ERN number is 02630431.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Dr. Mujkanovic, take a look at this -- take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's dated the 13th of June, 1992. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature in my document is covered by a stamp. I think you probably share my impression. It's impossible to recognise this signature, plus it's a bad copy too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's give a chance to the public to see the signature on the ELMO. Yes, okay, you can hand back the document to the witness, Madam Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The next document, P270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, the purpose of showing the witness the document was only to see if he could recognise the signature? That's all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: P270, bearing ERN number -- Your Honour, it is not easy to read it as such. 01 -- 018 - thank you - 01586. Your Honour, I have here the hard copy of the English translation of this document. I will hand it over to the usher for circulating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question to the witness is: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature resembles Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is document Srebrenica -- in the heading, "Srebrenica municipal Territorial Defence staff," dated, and I quote, "Srebrenica, 2 July 1992, decisions of the Territorial Defence staff."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I have a question related to the second paragraph, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. starting with a dash. There it is referring to a new-formed War Presidency. Are you aware with that formation as it existed upon your arrival in August 1992, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that, when I arrived, Hajrudin Avdic was president of the War Presidency, Hamdija Fejzic was president of the executive council, Dzemo Becirevic was the head of the economics department. Becir Bogilovic, I met him as the chief of the public security station in Srebrenica. Jusuf Halilovic was in civilian protection affairs. I don't know this man called Resid Efendic. Haziz Hekic or Mekic, I don't know the person. I don't know Mirsad Urbic. As for Senaid Tabakovic, I met him later. He was one of the local commanders. Sefik Mandzic, no. And it says here that Naser Oric was commander of the TO staff of Srebrenica. That was not his capacity as I knew it. The way I believed at the time, he was the commander of the Srebrenica defence forces. That was his official title, to my knowledge. I have never seen this document -- I hadn't seen this document until a year ago, when it was first shown me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to stop you here. My question still -- I have another question related to this War Presidency. Was Naser Oric, in your knowledge, part, a member, of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- Mirsad Halilovic, was he functioning as a commander of the wartime military police, as referred to in the paragraph of the second dash?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him about two months after my arrival in Srebrenica. He was chief of the military police at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, number 107. That's ERN number 01087786. This is document under the heading "Crisis Staff of Srebrenica TO, Srebrenica, 2 July 1992, Report to the Republic Staff Sarajevo and Regional Staff Tuzla." Dr. Mujkanovic, do you recognise the signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document is P3. P3, ERN number 00926461. My question is: Do you recognise this signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of the signature is covered by a stamp. If I look at the second part of the signature, it resembles Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 18th of October. Dr. Mujkanovic, I would like to address you to the second paragraph in which it is referring to constant communications by courier, and communications means from lower units to higher units and superior units -- and superiors by the 25th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the record, it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may correct for the record, in order to establish it, it's not stating that it's happening. It's not clear that from the way it was read. In order to establish constant communication, it's not suggested that that's happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that that's happening. I haven't asked any question. I have only, Your Honour, referred to the paragraph, and I referred to the content. I haven't put any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's for the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My learned friend can address something that happens and speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not speculating, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please stop, both of you. Mr. Wubben, proceed with your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was correcting the record, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware that ever since the 25th of October, 1992, or shortly later on, communications by couriers and communications -- or other communications from lower units to higher units and superiors have been implemented, or were functioning, as such?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or not. It has to be an open question. Are you aware that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have to make an allowance that the English that Mr. Wubben speaks is not to the same level that you do, Mr. Jones. But I think it's enough for the witness to understand what he's being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to understand it. I'm concerned that there's a continual attempt to put words in this witness' mouth, and that's why I insisted from the start that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case. I think it's clear enough. He's being asked whether he was aware of such communications taking place, which basically he's got the two alternatives. They may or may not, and he may or may not have been aware, so it's up to the witness to tell us what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with this order, nor did I know at the time that different units communicated by messengers. I don't know if this was the established practice that they used or if messengers were only used sporadically. I can only say that, for the most part, people communicated by courier. There were no electronic or telephone links. I can't comment on this order specifically because I was simply not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will proceed with another issue. Dr. Mujkanovic, did there come a time later on in 1992 that differences of opinions within -- within the members of the operations staff of the armed forces in Srebrenica existed?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that, in 1992 and 1993, the priority was to defend Srebrenica and try to have some sort of a normal life in the area. Obviously, people had their differences, and these differences were reflected in a number of ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also reflecting during meetings in the operations staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I only rarely attended meetings of the operations staff. Although I was a member, my duties at the hospital were of far greater importance. Very often one of my associates would go to one of those meetings, Dr. Avdo Hasanovic or Dr. Ilijas Pilav, whenever I asked them to go there and attend meetings, in case there was something to be discussed about the medical service and organising the war hospital to enable us to work as efficiently as was possible at the time, and under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, you already stated that yesterday, this kind of information, but my question referred to any differences of opinion within the operations staff. Let me be more specific, came that to a kind of climax at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Climax? I'm not sure what you mean by climax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there such a tension that the difference of opinions within the operations staff led to certain decisions to leave the operations staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that there was a faction within the operations staff. They were not happy with their status as members. These people went as far as to resign at one point, regardless of which they continued with their jobs until their eventual appointments to other duties and other jobs, which is something that occurred later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, can the witness -- can the witness be more specific, please? What -- who he's referring to, and what was the substance of this difference of opinions. It seems that at -- he's telling us that at some point in time, these divergences that existed there came to a head, and some members opted out, opted to leave the operations staff. I mean, can we know who they were and why they left? I mean, what was the substance of the disagreement with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document to confront the witness with, and I would like to show it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies for not having read your mind, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can the witness first answer who the people are and what the differences were? Otherwise he gets the document and it's suggested to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think you're right. Who were these people who eventually decided to leave the operations? Can you name them, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ramiz Becirevic, Nijaz Masic. I think there was another member or two of the operations staff who were unhappy about their own status within the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What was the substance of the complaint or of the disagreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly speaking, they did not have the vehicles they needed to go around and tour the different locations. That was what they complained about, roughly speaking. I was not part of that group myself, which makes it very difficult for me to say why they made the moves that they did, and eventually resigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben, you can -- you may now show the witness whatever document you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have one question first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a referring in the questions to you, Dr. Mujkanovic, to leaving the staff. Was it first -- at least first a move of a resignation to leave -- a resignation from the operational staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I said those people resigned, submitted their resignations. But I also told you that they carried on with their jobs after their resignations until they were eventually assigned to other tasks. For example, Mr. Wubben, Ramiz Becirevic, in February 1992, received his appointment as chief of the operations staff. Up until then, he had been with the training and education section. He had resigned, but he had not stopped working. And this applies also to all the others who handed in their resignations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Usher, may I have your assistance, please. Document P255. That's ERN 01839515.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, would you please read this document, and specifically the heading within the statements of reasons, under paragraph 1, the second part of it.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that second part of paragraph 1, starting with "The decision said that we were responsible," et cetera, referred further in this part of paragraph 1, "we are afraid of the truth that the War Presidency does not know the most basic competencies and hierarchy in the armed forces." Can you comment on that? Are you familiar with that information, this kind of opinion-sharing within the operations staff, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the opinion of the operations staff, as such. This was an opinion expressed by the individuals who signed this. Secondly, this document shows precisely what I've been trying to tell the Trial Chamber all along; namely, during the Srebrenica disaster, or the downfall of Srebrenica, in 1992 and 1993, neither the civilian bodies nor the military bodies were ever organised in a way that was prescribed by law. You did not know who was superior or who was subordinate to whom, or what fell under the jurisdiction of the civilian bodies and of the army respectively. This was a scene of total chaos, where no one knew who they were responsible to and for what. It was unclear who was making the appointments, or who was being appointed, for that matter. If one of these people believed that mistakes had been made about certain appointments, then this merely expresses the opinion of the individuals who signed this document. They may as well have been right. But that was not the point. There was no one there who would help us and clarify the procedure to appoint persons to certain positions. All the people left in the area were illiterate, the general level of education being very low. The highest level usually encountered was secondary school education. There was simply no one that was in a position to provide any clarification regarding these regulations. If I may be allowed to complete my clarification, because this may be of help for my testimony. I had more than enough reasons to hand in my resignation, I had more than enough reasons to leave, because there was no one that could make it possible for me to continue to work at the hospital under normal and satisfactory conditions. But I had to carry on. It was very simple: I had to carry on for the sake of my patients and because of everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We need to have a break now. We will resume at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, may I address you to the document on the ELMO, P255. And you have the originals in front of you, so the ELMO is in English, I presume. At the end, there is the naming of five persons, and above that --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above that it says, "The Staff members hereby sign their resignation." Are you familiar with these persons?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this consistent with your experience, that the persons named under 1, 3, and 5 also resigned?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are five people mentioned here, and there are four signatures. I've said that these people continued performing their functions to which they were appointed in the operations staff. The mere fact that they resigned didn't mean that they stopped working in the operations staff of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, I mean, I don't want anyone to be misled, even though there's a simple explanation to it. In your question, line 5, you told the witness, "and you have the originals in front of you." What he has in front of you, I'm informed, is not the originals but the document that we have in our record, that the Trial Chamber has in its record. So perhaps for -- just to be precise --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you have got all -- these alternatives: Either you tell him that that is a copy of what you contend is the original, or that -- or you show him the original straightaway. And let's see it on the ELMO as well so that we can verify what he has just testified in particular, because we --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for pointing this out. I rely on the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You rely on the copy. And you agree that, although there are five names, there are four signatures?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In the English translation, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, in the original. What I mean to say is that in the original that you have in your records, you agree that there are five names mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And four signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And four signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I -- my question related to the five names, and the witness, in my opinion, answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But in the English translation that is put on the ELMO, it purports to indicate that there are not only five names but that there are also five signatures. In actual fact, there are only -- that is a mistake that shows up in the English version of this document, and for the record, it's not correct that behind Mr. Adil Muhic's name, there is also his signature, because indeed there isn't; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed, because, for the record, that was essential to register. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will move now to another issue. Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware, if so, that there were any military operations done by the Srebrenica armed forces during the time of your stay in Srebrenica from August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these military operations offensives, or do you refer to those as combat attacks or another name?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the whole situation, there were such military operations that constituted the defence of Srebrenica from the attack of the aggressor. There were also attacks by the armed forces of Srebrenica on the territories that were held by the Serbs. I wouldn't call those either offensives or any other particular military terms. Those were operations that were carried out in the direction of some territories that had been occupied by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please -- can you please list the dates and areas of military operations by the armed forces of Srebrenica, at your time of your stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the attack operations or the defence operations which were undertaken by the armed forces of Srebrenica against the territories held by the Serbs? I can't remember the dates, but I can refer you to the period or the month when this happened. The first one was in the second half of September, in the place called Podravanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a matter of interpretation. I understand the witness is saying "akcija," which is being translated as "operations." Perhaps it's something the booth can help us with. We would have thought that "akcija" should be interpreted as "actions." It may matter because operations may imply a degree of planing which the word "action" doesn't -- doesn't have. But I understand the witness is saying "akcija" rather than "operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I disagree with counsel. Also an action can be planned and prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely and action can. But -- anyway, I'm asking the witness: Would you make a distinction between an operation and an akcija, or do they mean the same thing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not the same for me. An operation implies a well-planned activity which means that all the levels are well articulated, all the levels of command and control. And there is a very well-known reason why some communications are established, why some territories are linked up. An operation involves actions, military actions, at a wide scale. In this particular case, I'm talking about certain actions, the goal of which was to try and get food, primarily food, medicines, as well as weapons which, after such an action, might be seized and placed at the disposal of those individuals who did not have any arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question that was put to you by Mr. Wubben specifically referred to operations. How was the word "operations" translated from English into the B/C/S? Perhaps the operators behind -- in the booths can tell me. I think it would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did say "actions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how did you translate the word "operations"? Which word did you use in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We used "operacija" for operations, and for actions we used "akcija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need to put some order here. And before I move to explain what I expect from you, Witness, or the way to approach this particular chapter of your testimony, I also need to -- need you to answer a question. You've just heard me ask the interpreters how they translated to you, how they interpreted to you, the word "operations," which was the word asked by Mr. Wubben in his question. And they told me that they used the word "operacija," which basically shouldn't have left any doubts in your mind as to what Mr. Wubben was referring to. You have obviously made a distinction in your mind between operacija and akcija, and in your answer you referred to what you described as akcija. Now, are you telling us that the military activity that you were a witness of during your stay in Srebrenica, there were no such thing as military operations but only military akcija? Is this what you are hinting to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. I can illustrate this with another example which might clarify things even further. If we are to talk about operations, an operation would imply, for example, linking up the free territory of Srebrenica with the free territory of Tuzla. In this specific case, such an operation would involve two units or two formations or two parts of the armed forces, and they would join forces on a joint project and they would advance from two different directions. The goal of that would be to establish a corridor between the Srebrenica territory and the Tuzla territory. This would be a well-coordinated military operation. When it comes to the armed forces of Srebrenica, I believe that it is pointless to talk about operations. Those were actions taking place in the course of one day. People would break through the enemy lines in order to get food. They would break those lines and primarily take food. Later on, they would also take some other things that they required. They would leave those territories without anybody subsequently controlling them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So basically, there are no military operations that you are prepared to talk about, but only military actions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was clear, and I explained what an operation is and what an action is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my next point is, of course, I cannot take over, I direct myself again to you, rephrase your question, and there is no point in asking the witness to tell us about military operations, you can only ask him about military actions. The way I suggest we go about this is this: We'll give the witness as much space is possible. What I suggest, rather than doing it by question and answer, I would give you the floor, Dr. Mujkanovic, and I would ask you to try and remember as many of these military akcija as you can. Take them one by one. If it is possible to take them in a chronological fashion, manner, that's better; if you cannot, it's not a problem. Take them in which ever manner you like. But concentrate on one action at a time. And when you're doing so, please tell us whether, in your opinion, it was of an offensive or of a defensive nature. And of course, Mr. Wubben, if you, at any time, would like to interrupt the witness, please draw our attention, but try not to interrupt him unless we give you the go-ahead. Then of course you are free to put all the questions at the end, or if you prefer, at the end of each akcija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I prefer first to have him recall the various actions on dates and areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The akcijas, yes. Yes, Dr. Mujkanovic, you've got as much time as you like, or as you need, to tell us about these military actions, that you are aware of, obviously, I mean. Please give us all the details that you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, before Dr. Mujkanovic proceeds, what I mentioned with my last remark is that he first give us an overview of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- and then further on, the details of -- so first a list, and then working through the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's take a list and see what you can remember, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he already started with -- referring to an action in the Podravanje, as I recall it, the second half of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't testify for him. Let him testify. He knows, I suppose, where he left before I spoke.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of September, there was an action in Podravanje, between the free territory of Srebrenica and the free territory of Zepa, that is, a village between those two villages. Sometime in October, there was another action in the area of Fakovici, which is a village on the Drina River. I believe that sometime in December there was another action in the area of the villages of Voljevica, Zaluzje, Bjelovac, and Loznica, Rijeka. Those are Muslim villages which had been occupied by the Serbs in 1992, at the beginning of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the beginning of January, there was another action in the area of Kravica, and sometime in mid-January there was an action in the area of Skelani, in the south-east part of the municipality of Srebrenica. Those were the offensive actions. The Defence actions took place as soon as I arrived in the area. There was a general attack on the defence lines in the Suceska area. There were daily attacks by the aggressor on the defence lines of the Srebrenica enclave. In mid-February 1993, an attack started and lasted until the 17th of April, 1993. There was a general attack on Srebrenica from various directions, and this attack involved the forces of the JNA, the air force, the long-range artillery from the territory of Serbia. Those were the actions that took place in the territory of the Srebrenica enclave. As far as I can remember, and I remember these actions not because I participated in them but because I received wounded from those localities when these actions were taking place. And as the medical corps, we had to organise the receipt of the wounded from the place where they were wounded to their arrival in the Srebrenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we take them one by one? Is it important for the Prosecution to take them one by one? I would imagine that it is. Also for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take the offensive ones, the ones you have described as offensive. The first one, September, Podravanje, what can you tell us about that action.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this action lasted just one day. The man reason why this action took place was to get hold of the bare necessities, which was food and medical supplies for the hospital, and also to get hold of some weapons that -- and ammunition that was required for the quality defence of the Srebrenica enclave. This was the first time ever that I visited the place where an action took place. Two or three days later, after the action was completed and the locality was taken, I joined members of the Hakija Meholjic unit in Srebrenica. I arrived in Podravanje. Why I went there was to try and get information about the possible existence of an out-patient clinic with drugs and medical supplies. And the unit went there in order to mop up the area, to inspect the area and see whether there were any left-over enemy groups in the area. They also wanted to see whether there were any places where weapons were stored. They wanted to see whether there were any wounded members of the Serbian army there. The overall goal was to look after the wounded and take the food and medical supplies which were to be -- which were to be used in the territory of the enclave, which were to be used by the civilians and the army. While I was in that locality, from the morning of that day until late afternoon, I managed to see a lot of people who were there. There were lots of civilians, women, children, elderly. They were searching the houses, looking for food. Some were also taking some other things, such as TV sets and refrigerators. They loaded those things on horse carts. I saw people digging through yards and gardens. I asked them what they were looking for. They told me that they were looking for ammunition or food or some other things that may have been buried in the ground. I also saw people poking the surface of the soil with iron rods. They told me that they were looking for boxes or similar things that might have been buried in the ground. I also saw people who were digging in the ground that had already been dug out. They were looking for something, I don't know what. As I was passing by the Gunjaci bauxite mine - I believe this is the name of the mine - I saw a depot or a warehouse which was fenced off. And in that depot, there were barrels of motor oil. I saw people taking those barrels and loading them onto horse carts. I also saw people pushing wheelbarrows and loading stuff onto those wheelbarrows. I also saw, as I was passing by, an excavator or which was used in the mine. I saw that people had torched this excavator. Before that, as we were passing by, I saw two men running across a hill slope. Since they were some 6 or 700 metres away from me as the crow flies, I asked Hakija to look through his binoculars and see who these people were. I thought that they might be soldiers of the Serbian army. And when I looked through the binoculars, I saw two men in civilian clothes. They were not armed. They ran up to a haystack, and maybe two or three minutes later, I could see smoke coming from the top of that haystack. Hakija cried out towards them and told them not to torch the hay, and they replied that it was Cica who ordered them to do that. Cica was Zulfo Tursunovic. All these people who were there, they continued searching the houses, collecting the stuff that they needed. Some were even taking off window frames from the houses because they needed those frames. In Srebrenica, I've already told you that there was constant shelling in Srebrenica, that window-panes and window glass had been shattered by the shell shrapnel. That's why people were taking off window frames from those houses in order to take them back home and to use them on their houses. I also saw a few houses that started burning at the time. I have to say that except for the unit of Hakija Meholjic, there were no other members of the army, there were only women, children, and elderly, and they were all collecting stuff and taking it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I mean, he's your witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, you mentioned the name of Zulfo. Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He mentioned the nickname of Zulfo, not the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, and then referring to the linkage with the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, are you aware, what units did participate in that attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please confirm to the Trial Chamber the units and their commanders, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I didn't have the information. I don't know which units exactly participated, but I know that wounded persons kept coming in, mostly -- I can tell you according to the respective localities of the wounded. Most of them were coming in from the Suceska area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is linked as a unit to the Suceska area, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the full name of Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you also knowledge about any participation in this attack by Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of his participation or his role in this action in the Podravanje area. Podravanje is a localisation that is adjacent to Suceska. The wounded persons that I received, whenever a wounded person came in, their names, first, last names, and years of birth, would be registered in our medical files. A person would be marked as an army member or a civilian. Wounded in such and such localisation or during an attack against a certain area or defence of a certain area. That was the kind of medical files that we had, and this is how Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information was registered. So we always knew where a certain wounded person had come from, and we would always know whether this person was a civilian or an army member, whether the person was wounded during an act of defence or attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after this offence action in the Podravanje area, you did not treat any wounded in the hospital, or am I incorrect?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, in the hospital. All those who were wounded were brought into the hospital, all of them. I said that, two or three days after the action was over, that I visited the area. Once my work at the hospital was done, once we had provided adequate treatment to all the persons who were wounded, I went out and reached the area in order to see if I could get any more medical supplies and medicines. I'd been told that there was a mine over there in the area, and this led me to believe that there was some sort of a medical institution, a health centre or something like that, a place where I would be able to possibly obtain medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question, Dr. Mujkanovic: When you treated those patients in the hospital after this action, offence action, did you find out about their background, from what unit they were, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, most of them were from Zulfo Tursunovic's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also -- did you speak with those patients?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always spoke to our patients, but they were a rather unreliable source of information. You must know that those people were wounded or injured. Their perception of what's going on was rather different from what was actually happening. They suffered an enormous amount of stress. They were prone to exaggerate or disfigure certain events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to an offence action like this, did you prepare, together with the staff, prepare such an action with a view to the wounded who might be projected [sic]?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that, as the medical corps, we always prepared to receive men who were wounded in a certain action. We had our outposts in a number of different localities in the enclave. Those were wartime surgical outposts, mostly manned by nurses and medical technicians. Whenever there was an armed conflict, we would always cover the area by sending off an extra doctor to be on stand-by in the area so that the wounded might be taken care of and helped as swiftly as possible, and to make sure they survived the transport to Srebrenica, so that they could then be given further medical assistance once they reached the hospital. The transport sometimes took as long as several hours, since the distances were rather great. Some people didn't make it to the hospital. Sometimes, if a particular transport took three or four hours, people would die on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I take it that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, so can I take it as a conclusion that you used to be warned prior to such an -- such a military action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that we, the medical corps, were not involved in organising or planning any action. We would only be told to prepare, to prepare our operating theatres and to set up outposts for certain actions. The medical corps had nothing to do with planning or, in any other way, being involved in any of the actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who updated you, then, of such a planned action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would usually be the hospital manager, Avdo Hasanovic. He was the one who was called. Once back, he would tell us to start getting ready to prepare the medical corps, to prepare the facilities, because an action would soon be under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move to the following attack on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I used the word "attack," but I must use the word, to be correct, military action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a question of the witness on Podravanje. I'm looking at the statement you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, and at a certain point you were asked, and you listed these offensives, akcija, as you put it, and you said: "Let me speak about the actual offensives. First, I will list them." And you start listing them, you start with September, Podravanje; October, Fakovici; November, Kamenica, December, Muslim villages occupied by the Serbs, Voljevica, Bjelovac, Kunarac, Loznica, Rijeka and Sase; January, Kravica area, and again towards the end of -- mid, end of January, Skelani, Jezero. And then you make a very categoric statement to the Prosecutor. And then you say: "Naser was physically at each and every one of these offensives, directing them."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I. This witness hasn't adopted this statement, he hasn't been asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm going to ask him whether to accept this or to deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may I also -- there's a matter, if his priority statements -- if he's going to be cross-examined on his prior statements, there's a matter I would like to discuss in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later. At the moment he's being confronted with a statement which runs counter to what he has testified contrary so far. So I'm going to confront him with it and I need an answer from the witness. And then we'll discuss what you need to discuss later, Mr. Jones. Yes, I'm putting it to you that, in your statement of 2000, you said or you stated that Naser was physically at each and every one of these offensives, directing them. Today you told us that you do not recall Naser, or you excluded categorically, Naser ever being present during the attack or the offensive, the Podravanje offensive. Which is the correct version of these two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that he was there or that he wasn't. What I said is that I did not personally see him there. As for my statement, and the way it was drawn up, that's a different thing altogether. Maybe we can discuss that on another occasion. The crux of the matter is I never said that Naser was physically present in each of these offensives, or indeed that he led the actions. I did say yesterday that, after every action, he would come to the hospital to talk to the wounded. And it was possible to draw the conclusion, based on the conversations that he had with the patients and with me, that he had been physically present in these actions. But I can't say that I saw him being there. I can't say that. And you must know, I'm under oath here. I am only entitled to say what I saw with my own eyes and not talk about hearsay, about things that I merely heard from someone else. When I talked about Podravanje, I talked about what I saw with my own eyes. As concerns all the other actions, I was never there, I wasn't even in the area. Therefore, the only thing I can talk about is the wounded that kept coming in, the way these people were treated. I can also tell you what the conclusions were that I drew based on my conversations with the patients, if that's of any importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Wubben, we'll move to the next offensive, Fakovici, October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Before we address to that issue, I would like to have a private session, Your Honour - it won't take long - without the witness. It does not refer to the witness, it refers to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime, you can raise the other matter that you mentioned too. Witness, could you please -- you're going to be escorted out of the courtroom for a while. We need to discuss a few things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Mr. Jones, you said you wanted to raise a matter relating to his statement not in the presence of the witness. The witness is not here. Perhaps you can refer to it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please slow down and make a short break between each other because we can't follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We ought to practice what we preach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might be premature, so I won't embark on it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's really a question of if the witness was going to be, as I say, cross-examined on his prior statements, there were submissions we would want to make in that regard, but we haven't got there yet, so it's now -- it's premature at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Usher, could you bring in the witness again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry about that, Dr. Mujkanovic, but we needed again to discuss a procedural matter. And Mr. Wubben will be proceeding with his direct, with his examination-in-chief, and I think we had come to the stage where we were about to start discussing the Fakovici offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct.
