utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I would like to move to that offensive action related to Fakovici. Will you please tell the Court, in the same way as you did on the prior action, what your knowledge is about that military action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at the beginning of October 1992. An action was carried out in the village of Fakovici, which is on the Drina River. This is the eastern part of the Srebrenica enclave. I know that I received up to 15 wounded after that action, among whom was also Zulfo Tursunovic, who was also wounded and who was brought to the hospital. The action also took one day. And what I found interesting at the time is that after that action, we received some medicines and medical supplies at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been updated prior to the attack? I will rephrase that. Have you been, as a medical doctor organising the war hospital, updated prior to this action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given a signal that there would be an action. We were not given any detail. We were just told to prepare ourselves. And the day before the action itself, before the action took place, we reinforced our surgical outposts in the south-eastern part of the Srebrenica enclave. At the beginning of the action, a doctor was sent to reinforce this outpost that was closest to the area and which received the wounded from the area. You have to know that these actions that were organised were organised in secrecy. Nobody could know about these actions because there was always a risk that the civilians learned about the action in the area and they placed themselves on the border of that area which gave them an opportunity to get into the village as soon as possible and find food. I received many more civilian casualties than military casualties, and that is why we were never told in advance when and where the action would take place. It was only at the beginning of the very action, once all the preparations had been over, that a doctor would be called to a certain outpost to treat the wounded there. And this is how the things functioned at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, when you speak about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, when you tell the Judges it was organised in secrecy, who did organise this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I've said that it was done in secrecy, that means that I was not privy to the information. I'm not a witness who could tell you who the organisers were. Sometimes those actions were organised by the units closest to the particular areas. I was not involved in the organisation of any military actions or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who updated you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who updated you prior to that action? Who gave you the signal?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been Dr. Avdo Hasanovic, who was the director of the hospital. It could have also been the chief of the operations staff, Mr. Osman Osmanovic. It could have been somebody from the War Presidency. It was not always one and the same person who was in charge of the correspondence between the war hospital and the rest of the War Presidency, or the rest of the army, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric, after this military offensive action, also visit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always came to the hospital after all the actions, regardless of the nature of the action. That was just his habit. He would come, visit the wounded, have a chat with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to Naser Oric on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him very often. Whenever he came to the hospital, we would talk, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn from Mr. Naser Oric or from the soldiers who participated in that action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were not a reliable source of information on the action that had taken place. They were too subjective and they provided us with incorrect information. Sometimes they would say that there were dozens of dead soldiers, or they would say that the line had been broken and that they entered the village, whereas the truth was completely different. It was only later on, when things calmed down and when we started talking to them, we could tell that those actions were always dangerous, that there were a lot of casualties, a lot of dead and wounded. When Naser came, we usually discussed the weapons that had been seized. His main interest was to have enough ammunition and weapons for the army. I've already told you that civilians who went there would storm into the villages during the action to get hold of the food. And then when such civilians would be brought to the hospital wounded, I would ask them what they were looking for there, and they said to us that they wanted to get hold of the food. Naser would inquire after some people, especially about those who were seriously wounded. He wanted to know whether these people would survive, whether they would be handicapped after that. And this is more or less what my conversations with him boiled down to. If a village was taken, and if certain quantities of ammunition, weapons, and food were taken from the village, then everything was really euphoric and happy, because this was the only means of survival. There were no logistical supplies. Nobody brought as much as a kilo of flour or litre of oil into Srebrenica, and still people had to live. These actions were all undertaken in order to enable people to survive, not to take territories. Those territories were not needed by anybody. When the actions were over, nobody remained living in the territory. Nobody wanted or could stay there. We could not hold such a huge territory. When the action was over, the army withdrew, the civilians lingered on for a few days. They searched the houses, they got hold of the necessities which then they either used or exchanged or sold on the black market. The area of Srebrenica was not fit for any organised life. There was no judge, there was no teacher, there were no lawyers, there was nobody there. There was just people, poor people, who had already been expelled two or three times before they reached Srebrenica. And there was nothing there to offer to them. There was no ammunition, there was no weapons, no clothes, no accommodation, so people organised themselves as best as they could. Srebrenica is more a sociological issue than an issue which could serve for an analysis of organisation. Srebrenica did not have any means of functioning the way one would want it to function. All the military developments and the military authorities were just part of the organisation put together by individuals in certain villages, and the only -- the objective of these individuals was to protect themselves against any further persecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I would like to ask you, when you start by explaining what the patients might have said to you, or shared information with you afterwards, my next question is: What did you learn after this military action from Naser Oric, upon his visit to the hospital? And meaning, what did you learn regarding the participation of units and commanders in this attack, in this military action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, let me say this: Today we're talking about the events which took place 12 or 13 years ago, and the fact that a person forgets is part of his physiological process. Sometimes people can't remember two or three years ago, let alone things that happened 12 or 13 years ago. And Srebrenica is not the only thing that happened in my life, and I do not have a photographic memory. There is no way for me to remember everything that happened there. I'm trying to reconstruct some things, I'm trying to recall some things. And if I'm certain about things the way I remember them, I will say so. If I'm not sure or I cannot remember, then I believe that this Trial Chamber does not want me to talk about those things. What happened 12 or 13 years ago, what Naser told me at the time, I don't think that I can be a credible witness to that. I cannot remember certain events. If I told you that I spoke about girls with Naser, he was a normal young man who had other needs. It was not his only need to defend the people in the area. We may have spoken about girls as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. My question was only related to what you really might know, so if you don't know, please be confident to express that as such. And what I'm interested in is, indeed, what you can recall.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember these conversations that I had with Naser after these actions. Despite all my efforts, and despite my wish to help the Trial Chamber, I really cannot say that this was -- this was precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is, Dr. Mujkanovic: You recall that Zulfo was wounded. Can I take it that he was wounded due to this military action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was wounded during that military action, and this is what I can remember. He came to me as a patient, and he told me that he had taken part in the attack on Fakovici together with other members of his unit, the part of the unit that was involved in this action on Fakovici. This is something that I cannot deny. He was wounded; this is a fact. He was wounded in Fakovici, and this is part of his medical record. If you have those medical records, I believe that you can easily check that this was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Mujkanovic, did Zulfo Tursunovic also share with you information of other units involved?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'd like to have the assistance of the usher, please. I would like to show Dr. Mujkanovic a document numbered P2. P2, Your Honours, with ERN number 00926396.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, do you recognise this signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, and I quote, is an order "Subregional Armed Forces Staff," and the date, 11th of December, 1992. May I draw your attention to the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There it is referring to carry out a frontal attack on an axis. And are you familiar with that frontal attack as mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph there is an appointment of Semso Salihovic. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this? Is this a commander or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the commander of Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is referring to an attack on a certain date, in the first paragraph, the 14th of December. Is it possible that this refers to one of the military actions you yourself referred to in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The places that are mentioned here, they are not part of the area which -- are in reference to the actions that I spoke about as having taken place in 1992. This is the area of Cerska. This is not part of Srebrenica, this is separate from Srebrenica, in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear. In other words, Voljevica, Bjelovac, Kunarac, Loznica, Rijeka, and Sase would not fall within this geographical area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I draw your attention, Dr. Mujkanovic, on the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I quote: "On 14 December 1992, carried out a frontal attack on the village of Zeljkovici. Does that frontal attack refer to any military action you referred to in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May have I the assistance of the usher for the next document. It's document number P13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's an -- will you please, Dr. Mujkanovic, take a look at the signature. Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This signature looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an -- this is an order, and I quote, "Srebrenica Armed Forces," dated 11th of December, 1992. There is an order, and I quote "for all members of the armed forces of Srebrenica," with the naming of places, "are to be transferred from their home units to the unit commanded by Dzenanovic Hazim." Are you familiar with the implementation of that order, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I even don't know who this Hazim Dzenanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that this order is related to a military action, as referred to you in your prior statement, in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It seems to me the question was inviting him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I also don't understand correctly what -- what do you mean, your prior statement, in December --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, I mean prior statement, testimony before the Court, he referred to a military action, offensive action, in December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- and mentioned several places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That were Serb territory at the time -- Serb-occupied territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So that's what -- and if the witness doesn't know, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very clear question now. In looking at this document that you have in front of you, do you think that this document refers to the offensive that you mentioned earlier on in your testimony, namely, the December one, which concentrated on Voljevica, Bjelovac, Kunarac, Loznica, Rijeka, and Sase? Or is it something different? Because here we see that Voljevica is there. Bjelovac is there. Zaluzje, you mentioned it as well, yes? Biljaca, you had not mentioned before. So the only one you did not mention is Biljaca. Before, when I went down my notes, you mentioned Voljevica, Zaluzje, Bjelovac, Kunarac, Loznica, and Rijeka. So does this document really, in your opinion, without speculating, refer to the offensive that you testified about earlier on, or not? Or could it be something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't be able to say what this document is about. I'm not familiar with the document, I'm not familiar with this order. And since you've told me not to speculate, my answer would be I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will now move, indeed, to that issue of the military action in December, as referred earlier by you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, would you please tell the Court, inform the Court, what you know about that military action in December 1992? And please concentrate in that respect on the military action, as far as you know, in the village of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This action took place in December 1992. The intention was to liberate occupied villages, occupied Muslim villages, along the Drina River. Voljevica, Zaluzje, Bjelovac, Loznica, Rijeka, and so on and so forth. Again, the main reason why the action was organised, why the attack was organised was to get hold of food, materiel, technical supplies, medicines, and everything else that was required for the normal functioning of the free territory of Srebrenica. The action lasted for two or three days, I don't know exactly. I know that I had a lot of wounded after that action. There were a lot of wounded civilians, very many wounded civilians. I know that the air force came from the direction of Serbia and opened fire on the people who were advancing towards these villages. I know that I had a lot of wounded who had been wounded from aeroplane. And once these villages were taken, once they were liberated, there was an attempt to organise life in this area, because people from this area had come as refugees to Srebrenica. However, this attempt failed because it was impossible to live along the River Drina with Serbia across the river. Life could not be organised because there was constant, everyday shelling from Serbia on those villages, on Voljevica and other villages. People stayed there for a very brief period of time, and then they abandoned the area and returned to Srebrenica. What I know - I apologise - I know from the stories of Safet Omerovic, who is a native of Voljevica. He told me that they, as a special purpose unit or a sabotage unit, in the course of the night they entered the territories that were occupied and the action started from the inside. The first wave of attack took place in the village itself. I don't know whether it was Biljaca or Bjelovac. That's how the action started, that's how the attack on that territory started. This is what I know, what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from a medical organising point of view, had you been warned in advance?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely in the same way as earlier. I can only say that, during that action, the first day, because people kept coming in with very unusual wounds, I couldn't tell exactly what had caused them. But then later on I saw aeroplanes, the air force, firing. There were rivers of people, 2.000 people, pushing towards those villages. Some came with horses. It was impossible to describe the scene. Ramiz Becirevic took me to the forward command post to have a clearer view of the area, and I realised that hundreds of thousands of people were moving towards the lines, once the lines had been broken through. On the way to the villages, I saw aeroplanes, fighter plains, come from Serbia firing on those people. I stayed there for up to one hour. I had to go back to the hospital because lots of wounded people kept coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, did you also find out what units took part, participated, in that attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were units adjacent to these village areas, units covering the defence line of the eastern section of the Srebrenica enclave, reinforced by units from Suceska and by units from Srebrenica, meaning Akif Ustic's and Hakim Emic's [phoen] unit. I am talking about the wounded that kept coming into my hospital. I am telling you where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you don't know the commander of those units, can you list the units involved that were adjacent to that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units were Likari, Pirica Brdo, that's what I think the name is, part of Pale, Gornji Potocari, and the ones I've mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ones you mentioned before on the attack on Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't speaking about those units when I spoke about Fakovici. I only said I knew about Zulfo Tursunovic's unit being involved because he was wounded as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my conclusion is correct that, his unit, or part of his unit, participated?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is my last question regarding this event. I will move now to the other after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break now, resuming at 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is another issue of the offensive actions. Dr. Mujkanovic, can you please tell the Court, inform the Court, what you know about the offensive military action in the Kravica area, in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of January 1993, there was an action on Kravica village. The action lasted approximately one day. During the action, the village was taken. And I know that it was winter, there was a lot of snow. And for days I could see people passing through Srebrenica and carrying or driving certain things that they had taken from the houses in Kravica. There was food, there were some things like TV sets, cookers, refrigerators, so on and so forth. There were not many wounded after that action. It was an action in which some 15 to 20 people were wounded and treated in the hospital on the same day. And this would be more or less what I can tell you about it, what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, were you also prior warned to prepare the hospital for casualties?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the way that I have already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who updated you of that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I can't remember. It was not always the same person who prepared us. We were informed, and we prepared ourselves. I can't tell you exactly who it was who informed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out after this offensive? What units did participate in this military action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were units from the area, from the area of Konjevic Polje which is adjacent to the village of Kravica. They were supported by the units from the area of Srebrenica, from parts of Glogova, a village next to Kravica, as well as some parts of other units from the area of Srebrenica. I will repeat once again, we're talking about the parts of units from Suceska and from the rest of the area leaning on Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be specific, if you can. Next to the Suceska unit, whether or not you can recall names of other units involved?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said that I can't remember the names of units that participated in certain actions. I'm just giving you what I recall. Based on the wounded who arrived at the hospital and based on their stories, more or less those were units from Konjevic Polje, Glogova, reinforced by some other units. Again, the same person who told me about the previous action, Safet Omerovic, told me that he also participated in this action in Kravica, and he told me that, again, the same way parts of the special purpose sabotage unit were infiltrated in the area of Kravica, that is how the action started, from the inside. And it was over in the course of one day. The village was taken. Civilians started scouring the village, they did it for days, and for days they were taking things out of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- issue of taking things, taking properties out of the village after such a military action, did only civilians participate in that? Or is it your knowledge whether or not also units, or parts of it, did the same practice?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that the troops took were weapons and ammunition. I've already told you that these actions were always accompanied by the presence of civilians who were waiting on the lines. As soon as the defence line was broken, they were the first ones to enter those villages and to start taking things, primarily food, cigarettes, if they found them. Civilians were not interested either in ammunition or weapons, and the troops needed ammunition and weapons. And the troops really didn't have the time to secure the area and prevent the break-in by civilians. So it was the civilians that demolished the whole area. And it is a well-known fact. Everybody who spent at least a month there can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. I have a curiosity which maybe you can clear for me, Dr. Mujkanovic. Earlier on, answering a question put to you by Mr. Wubben about these akcija, about these actions, you said, "You have to know that these actions that were organised were organised in secrecy," and you repeated it then later on. Can you explain to me, the presence of all these civilians, more or less at the same time that the attack or the action was taking place, if the organisation of these attacks was prepared in secrecy or was held in secrecy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody in Srebrenica could account for that. This is a problem that the War Presidency also discussed. Everybody was concerned as to how an action could be organised without the civilians learning about that. Soldiers lived in their houses. They did not have a barracks. They lived with their families in their households, and they all wanted to get hold of food. And although the actions were prepared in secrecy, I'm sure that they spoke about these actions in their households. They probably swore their household members to secrecy. But still they told them where to be in order to get food. So I suppose that the most plausible explanation would be that the troops shared the secret with their families. This is something that could not be prevented in Srebrenica. Civilians knew. After some actions, my first wounded to arrive in the hospital were the civilians, and they were only then followed by soldiers. Civilians were sometimes first to enter an area that had been liberated. These are facts. Everybody who was ever there can confirm that. This was, indeed, a problem. It was not so much the problem that people took food, it was -- and it was not premeditated by any ulterior motive. It was the survival instinct that pushed these people to enter those villages. They would light fires sometimes during the night, if it was cold. They were waiting for the army to start the action, for them to follow after the troops. It is a phenomenon that nobody who hasn't experienced it can understand, and it's very hard to explain. Sometimes civilians would enter these villages even before the troops, and sometimes many of them were wounded, many of them were killed, many of them did not accomplish their mission. They didn't get hold of the food, although it was food they came for in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mujkanovic. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, taking away properties is one thing you addressed and burning haystacks is another you recalled and testified upon. Do you also recall that people spoke about burning other properties, other properties than haystacks?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were burning all sorts of property. They were burning houses, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was burning houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilians. First, they would scavenge through a village, they would get whatever they could lay their hands on, and then they would burn houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you come to know --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw this happen in Podravanje, with my own eyes. I saw houses being set fire to by civilians, women, children, elderly people who were there. Hundreds of them would search the area, pick up whatever they could, and the last thing they would do is set fire to a house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a kind of practice also caused by soldiers of local units?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers did not burn any houses. The soldiers never even took any furniture away from the houses, or anything like that. As I said before, once a village was taken, civilians would flood the village before the army ever got there, and they would spend days scouring the area, removing roof tiles, woodwork, whatever they needed back in Srebrenica. They would take what they needed and they would burn the house down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these problems, the problem of taking away properties and burning of properties, including houses, had they been discussed during meetings? And I mean meetings between you and other staff or other commanders of the Srebrenica armed forces.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that this was perceived as a public problem in Srebrenica. This was discussed. I was not a member of the War Presidency, nor did I attend any of their meetings. I occasionally attended sessions of the operations staff, whenever time allowed. I know that this was one of the major problems, how to prevent the burning of property. But it simply wasn't possible. This was something that was definitely discussed. No one approved of this, no one approved of the burnings or the theft, but it wasn't possible to put an end to this because there were no instruments that we could use to prevent this from happening. This was definitely a burning problem. There were attempts, efforts, being made to move some of the refugees leaving Srebrenica to some of these villages that were retaken, because the living conditions were much better than the ones in Srebrenica, but they refused to. And one of the reasons why they were burning things might have been precisely that, to avoid being moved to those villages, probably because they did not feel safe. They probably only felt safe in and around Srebrenica, safe from enemy incursions. This is a phenomenon which was real, and there was nothing that could be done to stop this happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you -- Dr. Mujkanovic, what did you express as your opinion during those meetings regarding this problem? Did you express it in a way like you did to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only at meetings. There were lots of informal conversations that I had with people that I would run into, people from the War Presidency, members of the army, all sorts of people. I voiced my discontent. I said, "We should find a way to protect property." But there weren't enough soldiers to properly cover the village, to have people guard the houses. People were waiting right there along the defence lines. Once a village was taken, there was no one left there. They would always withdraw back to the lines from which the attack had originally started. This was a physical impossibility. There was no way to have any effective protection. However, some things were needed back in Srebrenica, such as roof tiles and woodwork. And I said, okay, if that's what it takes, they can have those things removed, moved to Srebrenica, have these things stored in Srebrenica, so that we could use these things after a shelling, when houses were damaged. But it didn't work like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you discussed this at -- occasionally at sessions of the operations staff, as you told the Judges. Did you also discuss that, or does that include a discussion with Naser Oric on those two problems?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the opinion of Naser Oric in that regard?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the same opinion. He was against people burning houses, but there was simply nothing that he could do. He did not have a way of stopping them. It's not that he simply didn't approve. He fiercely opposed this. But you must know that there were between 80.000 and 100.000 people living in the area. You couldn't keep all these people at bay. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, Dr. Mujkanovic, that you could predict in advance that this practice would occur on every offensive action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be predicted, it could be predicted that this would occur. But I also said that these civilians could simply not be held under control, the women and children who were the first to run to the houses in order to grab whatever they needed. These are simple facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Related to the issue of these military actions, you have explained to the Trial Chamber what you know about these actions that occurred in the months of October onwards to -- to January, and also with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you move into this, Mr. Wubben, during these -- it seems that you're telling us that this was quite discussed and debated amongst you, this matter of whether houses should be burnt down or not. Do you recall anyone who used to be in favour of burning down these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, there were people who believed that this was the proper thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember any specific names. But there was a feeling among some of the population, they favoured the burnings, and the argument was that if these houses were burned, the Serbs would not be able to go back. It was probably a need for revenge. You must keep in mind the fact that 70 per cent of the people in the Srebrenica area were refugees whose houses had been burned once, twice, three times. There were people who were vengeful. There were other people who believed that this was a way to prevent Serbs from retaking the area, posing a danger. But one thing is certain: There was no one living in those areas. Not Bosniaks, not the returning Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Mujkanovic. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, when these discussions took place, specific on the meetings of the operations staff in which you attended, as you said, occasionally, when did those discussions start? Was it from the beginning of the new staff as organised and discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussions started when Podravanje was taken. It was then that it became clear that some houses had been set alight, property, that sort of thing. That's what I know as to when these discussions began. Prior to that, I never witnessed or have taken part in any such conversations. We saw this at the time as a problem that had to be resolved in some way. Unfortunately, it proved impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I go back now in time of the day of your arrival in the beginning of August 1992. There you became -- you arrived, and do you also recall that at that time, that's the beginning of August, there had been or there were talks about another offensive or another action that took place, if you recall and as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the first 20 days I spent in Srebrenica at least, I didn't know many people. Maybe a handful, with the exception of the doctors and paramedics that I met when I came there, people I worked with. In the first few days, my task was to set up the hospital, to set up an operating theatre, to examine all the patients in the hospital, to perform what surgery I could, what operations I could. There were people there that had been in the hospital for as long as 40 or 50 days, patients that required operations, that required surgery. Believe me, I had no time. It was only after 20 days that I learned that Srebrenica had a centre, with a -- I thought that the place where they had the post office and the hospital, I thought that was the centre of town. It was only after 20 days that I found out about other streets being there, an extension of the settlement, with a centre proper. And I saw houses that had been burned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. I will put the question myself, because we're never going to end like this. Are you aware of an offensive which took place in the area of Andric at any time in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 6th of August, 1992, meaning not even one day following my arrival. A great number of wounded came in from Suceska because there had been an all-out attack against Suceska. Two days later, lots of wounded came in from another area. I wasn't sure if that had been an attack or an act of defence. But there were a lot of wounded who lost their legs when crossing minefields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, stop there for the time being. Do you have any further questions on this offensive, or on this akcija, call it whatever you like?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had that action any relationship with a village called Suzestica, as far as you know, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the interpretation I received, the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Jazestica. Jazestica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of the exact nature of the action. I don't know, therefore, if it was Jazestica or not. I really can't say. I didn't know at the time, nor did I find out later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you treated the wounded afterwards in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were lots of wounded, as I said, people who had strayed into a minefield. I had three surgical tables on which I performed parallel, leg surgery, amputations, with no anaesthetics, no pain-killers. People's forearms had to be amputated, people who had been fired at by an anti-tank gun. Two or three seriously wounded people were brought in in the late afternoon hours of that day. It was at about 3.00 or 4.00 that the wounded started coming in, and this continued until late at night. I remember that all too well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember that, can you also confirm to the Judges from what units they were, what local units?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any of those people, sir. I didn't even know all the people who worked with me. I can't possibly be expected to remember all the people from those units, and I wasn't even familiar with the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will move to the issue of uniforms, the wearing of uniforms by the local units, by the staff, by the armed forces of the Srebrenica -- the Srebrenica armed forces. Let me ask you some questions in that respect. Did the soldiers of the armed forces of Srebrenica, including the soldiers from a local unit, wear any uniforms, or did they wear other clothes, like civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll put it like this: A very small number, maybe 5 per cent of soldiers or people who were soldiers in the Srebrenica area had uniforms made up of a pair of trousers and a camouflage jacket. The rest of the armed forces wore civilian clothes, whatever clothes they had, trousers, pullovers, jackets. Those were no proper uniforms. It was just civilian clothes that people wore. Some of them had, for example, a pair of camouflage trousers over which they wore civilian clothes, or vice versa, a combination of a camouflage jacket with civilian trousers. The same applies to the shoes. Some had sneakers, some had specially woven village shoes. Some wore caps, some wore fur caps. Some wore insignia, the coat of arms of Bosnia at the time, six lilies in six fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there also a use of any distinction between local units, or in another matter, to make these kind of distinctions of what unit it was or what kind of action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for any distinguishing features, you couldn't tell who came from which unit. There was no way you could tell based on any of the insignia that they wore. I saw some soldiers who had been wounded and were then brought into the hospital. During certain actions, some wore armbands, white or a different colour. Sometimes they wore this armband in their lapel or around their arms. This was some sort of a mark or distinguishing feature to set them apart from everyone else and to mean that they belonged to a certain unit. But other than that, there were no distinguishing features. These armbands are pieces of cloth, usually between 35 and 40 centimetres long. It was a distinguishing feature, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it general -- excuse me. Was it a general practice to distinguish at least during actions, military actions, through bands or other material, that a certain number of members of the local units did participate in an action, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was worn by those units, or parts of units, that were launching an attack against a given village. This was not a mark of recognition between the different units but, rather, between the individuals that were involved in one and the same action, to prevent friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far, and I will move to another issue, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on whether you are in a position to conclude within three minutes, the next issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It will be short, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far, you mentioned the PTT building and the hospital. Can I please show you an aerial photograph of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Usher, may I have document P300, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, can you please indicate what buildings you recognise on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the centre of town right here. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one. I have to stop this. Do you have another copy of this aerial view, or not? Because this one you have tendered in evidence already. I imagine that once he is being asked to identify places that he knows, he needs to mark the document. And I would suggest a highlighter in a bright colour, like green or something like that, or red. That's orange. I don't think it's going to -- is it? And if we can't finish this in two minutes, let's leave it until tomorrow, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's wiser, because I thought you were just going to ask him about the PTT and the hospital, but your question was much wider than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I am familiar that it can be very short, Your Honour. Here I have the marker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please, Dr. Mujkanovic, show the main buildings that you know? Only limit it to the main buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mark them in a sequential order, number 1, and then we'll say what it is. Which is the first building that you identify on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]. This is the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has put a number 1, indicating what he believes to be the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]. This is the Domavija Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has put the number 2 next to what he believes to be the Domavija Hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]. This is the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has put the number 3 next to the location which he believes to be the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]. This is the Energoinvest building in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next to this building the witness has put the number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]. This is the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has put the number 5 against what he according to him is the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I have two questions to you, very short. Can you indicate the PTT building on this map?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not shown on the map, or the hospital for that matter. This is coming from the direction of Bratunac to the centre. The PTT building and the hospital are about 700 metres this away, on the road to Bratunac. Therefore, this map does not show the two buildings, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That finalises it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be given Prosecution Exhibit -- could you sign that map, please, Dr. Mujkanovic. What number should we give it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P493.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being given Prosecution Exhibit P493. Thank you. We will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
